    Earthquake or nuclear explosion?¶

    EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

    The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, opened for signature in 1996, bans every nuclear explosion, though it has not yet entered into force. A test can be hidden underground, out of sight, but the ground still shakes, and stations thousands of kilometres away record it. The trouble is that the Earth has thousands of earthquakes a year. To check a ban, you have to pick out the explosions among them, and you have to be right, because a false alarm accuses a country of breaking a treaty.

    Today you work with 1,118 real events from the International Seismological Centre's catalogue: 117 nuclear explosions and 1,001 earthquakes in the regions around the test sites. You learn how to score a rule when explosions are rare, how to keep that score honest, how to find a line that separates the two, and where to set the alarm. At the end of class you ask the line about five explosions it has never seen, North Korea's. At home you fit the line in one part of the world and check it in another.

    What you'll be able to do¶

    The science. Say why an explosion and an earthquake of the same size shake the ground differently, and which seismic measurement shows it; and judge a rule that flags explosions by the two mistakes it can make.

    Setup¶

    Run the next cell once. It reads the events, stored with the course: every event in three regions with test sites, plus North Korea, for which the International Seismological Centre (ISC) Bulletin lists both magnitudes this week uses. It splits off the five North Korean explosions into their own table, korea, for the end of class, and keeps the rest in events. It also reads the coastlines for the map, and makes grid, a table of points spread over the mb–Ms plane, for the probability map at the end of class, over the same mb and Ms range, 2 to 7, as the treaty's screening plot.

    1. How could a seismometer tell a test from an earthquake?¶

    An underground test. A nuclear device is placed hundreds of metres underground, at the bottom of a drilled shaft or at the end of a tunnel dug into a mountain, sealed in, and fired. Usually nothing reaches the surface but the shaking (and sometimes radioactive gas that seeps out), and later, often, a crater where the rock above the blast collapses. (Firing a device inside a large underground cavity can muffle the shaking many times over, one reason small tests are hard to find.)

    Left: a vertical underground test at the Nevada Test Site, the device at the bottom of a drilled hole. Diagram: US Government (public domain). Right: craters left at the Nevada Test Site where the ground collapsed into the cavities of underground tests. Photo: USGS (public domain). Both via Wikimedia Commons.

    Two sizes for one event. Shaking travels as waves. The fastest, the P waves, push and pull the rock along their path; S waves shake it from side to side; and the slow surface waves roll along the ground behind them.

    How each kind of seismic wave moves the ground: two body waves (P and S) and two surface waves (Love and Rayleigh). Figure: USGS (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

    An explosion pushes the rock outward from one small spot, the same in every direction, so most of its shaking leaves as P waves. An earthquake is two blocks of rock slipping past each other along a fault: it sends out strong S waves, and, because the slip spreads over a large patch of fault and lasts longer, strong surface waves too.

    North Korea's first test, 9 October 2006. Left: the test site (red star), earthquakes nearby (blue dots) and two seismic stations (triangles). Right: the explosion (red) and a recent earthquake nearby (blue) recorded at a station: the explosion's shaking is mostly P waves; the earthquake's largest shaking is its S waves. Figure: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Science & Technology Review (March 2009), via the Berkeley Seismological Laboratory blog.

    So seismologists give each event two sizes. The body-wave magnitude mb is read from the first, fast P wave. The surface-wave magnitude Ms is read from the slow surface waves that follow. A small, sudden source like an explosion puts little energy into those long surface waves, so for its mb, an explosion has a small Ms. That one sentence is the physics of the whole week; the rest is how to use it well.

    • the western US: 405 events, 36 of them explosions, 35 at the Nevada Test Site and one in Colorado;
    • Central Asia: 696 events, 64 explosions, 53 at the Soviet test site near Semipalatinsk (now in Kazakhstan) and 11 at China's Lop Nur;
    • Novaya Zemlya, an Arctic island where the Soviet Union also tested: 17 events, all explosions.

    Only events with both magnitudes are kept. Small explosions often have no Ms at all, so the table holds mostly large ones: only 9 of its 117 explosions have an mb below 5.4. Keep that in mind when the line meets smaller ones.

    2. How do we score a rule when explosions are rare?¶

    This is classification. In the regression weeks a model answered with a number. Here it answers with a label: explosion or earthquake. A guess is a column of True and False, one per event, from a rule or a model. It is scored against the label.

    The laziest rule is to say "earthquake" every time. It is the baseline, the simplest rule there is, scored first: a rule that cannot beat it does no useful work.

    ✏️ Your turn 1¶

    How good is "always earthquake"?

    Why: a score is only useful if a rule that does no work scores badly. Find out what the usual score, accuracy, gives the laziest rule.

    1. always_earthquake: a guess of False for every event, given. It is written as a mask on a column (no event has an mb above 100) so that it is a column of True and False like every other guess this week.
    2. accuracy: the share of events where the guess equals the label: the mean of the mask always_earthquake == events["is_explosion"]. The next line prints accuracy_score beside it.
    3. found: how many explosions the rule flags: the sum of the mask always_earthquake & events["is_explosion"].

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: accuracy and found.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    always_earthquake = events["mb"] > 100     # False for every event
accuracy = (always_earthquake == events["is_explosion"]).mean()
print("accuracy by hand:", round(accuracy, 3), "  with accuracy_score:", round(accuracy_score(events["is_explosion"], always_earthquake), 3))
found = (always_earthquake & events["is_explosion"]).sum()
print("explosions flagged:", found, "of", events["is_explosion"].sum())
    always_earthquake = events["mb"] > 100 # False for every event accuracy = (always_earthquake == events["is_explosion"]).mean() print("accuracy by hand:", round(accuracy, 3), " with accuracy_score:", round(accuracy_score(events["is_explosion"], always_earthquake), 3)) found = (always_earthquake & events["is_explosion"]).sum() print("explosions flagged:", found, "of", events["is_explosion"].sum())

explosions flagged: 0 of 117

    ✓ Your turn 1 — 'always earthquake' scores 0.895 and finds 0 explosions

    Accuracy 0.895, and not one explosion found. Nine events in ten are earthquakes, so a rule that never flags is right nine times in ten. When one label is rare, accuracy hides the misses. A treaty needs scores that count the two kinds of mistake apart.

    Four counts. Sort the events by label and by guess into four groups. A hit is an explosion the rule flagged, a miss an explosion it did not flag, and a false alarm an earthquake it flagged. The fourth group, earthquakes the rule leaves alone, is the right answer for most events. Two scores come from the counts:

    • precision = hits / (hits + false alarms): of the events you flagged, the share that were explosions;
    • recall = hits / (hits + misses): of the explosions, the share you flagged.

    F1 joins them into one number, $F_1 = 2PR/(P+R)$ with $P$ the precision and $R$ the recall, which is high only when both are high.

    Ten made-up events, two of them explosions, and the rule "flag every event with mb 5.7 or more":

print(ten_events)

    Count by eye: the rule flags the three events with mb 5.8, 5.9 and 6.2. One of them, 5.9, is an explosion: 1 hit and 2 false alarms. The explosion with mb 5.3 is missed. The six other earthquakes are left alone. So precision is 1 / (1 + 2) = 1/3, recall 1 / (1 + 1) = 1/2, and F1 = 2 × 1/3 × 1/2 / (1/3 + 1/2) = 0.4.

    confusion_matrix prints the same four counts as a table of 2 by 2: rows are the label (False, then True), columns the guess (False, then True). The names you will meet in other courses and papers: a hit is a true positive (TP), a false alarm a false positive (FP), a miss a false negative (FN), and an earthquake left alone a true negative (TN). Each score is read off one row or one column:

    ✏️ Your turn 2¶

    How well does a cut on mb alone find the explosions?

    Why: the simplest rule that looks at the data is a cut on one column. Scoring it uses all three new scores, which you compute from the counts yourself.

    1. guess_mb: True where an event's mb is 5.7 or more.
    2. hits, misses, false_alarms: the three counts, each as the sum of a mask. (guess_mb == False is the mask of the events not flagged.)
    3. precision_mb, recall_mb, f1_mb: the three scores from your counts, by the formulas above. The line after them prints what precision_score, recall_score and f1_score give for the same label and guess.
    4. The figure: histograms of mb for the earthquakes and the explosions, with a line at the cut.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: hits, misses, false_alarms, precision_mb, recall_mb and f1_mb.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    label = events["is_explosion"]
guess_mb = events["mb"] >= 5.7
hits = (guess_mb & label).sum()
misses = ((guess_mb == False) & label).sum()
false_alarms = (guess_mb & (label == False)).sum()
precision_mb = hits / (hits + false_alarms)
recall_mb = hits / (hits + misses)
f1_mb = 2 * precision_mb * recall_mb / (precision_mb + recall_mb)
print(hits, "hits,", misses, "misses,", false_alarms, "false alarms")
print("by hand:      precision", round(precision_mb, 3), " recall", round(recall_mb, 3), " F1", round(f1_mb, 3))
print("scikit-learn: precision", round(precision_score(label, guess_mb), 3), " recall", round(recall_score(label, guess_mb), 3), " F1", round(f1_score(label, guess_mb), 3))

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
bins = np.arange(3.65, 7.05, 0.1)     # one bin per tenth of a magnitude, the same for both
plt.hist(earthquakes["mb"], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, label="earthquakes")
plt.hist(explosions["mb"], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, color="red", label="explosions")
plt.axvline(5.7, color="black", label="the cut")
plt.xlabel("body-wave magnitude mb")
plt.ylabel("number of events")
plt.title("mb alone: the two labels overlap")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

    The cut finds 85 of 117 explosions, but it also flags 105 earthquakes: precision 0.447, recall 0.726, F1 0.554. The histogram shows why no cut on mb can do much better: big earthquakes and big explosions have the same mb. From here on the notebook calls f1_score, which does exactly the arithmetic you just did. A cut on Ms alone is worse:

    In [9]:

    3. How do we keep the score honest?¶

    Rule one: no column may already know the answer. Depth looks tempting: earthquakes start kilometres down, and a test hole is a few hundred metres deep.

    An F1 of 0.996, nearly perfect, and useless. All 117 explosions have depth 0.0, and the catalogue marks each of those depths as fixed by the analyst, not measured from the waves: the analyst set it to 0 because the event was already known to be an explosion. The column knew the answer before anyone looked. This is called leakage: a column that already holds the answer. When a score looks too good, first ask whether a column already knew the answer. (Shallow depths are hard to measure, so the catalogue fixed the depth of 343 earthquakes too, and depth cannot separate two shallow events.)

    Rule two: training, validation and test. You met this in the model-selection week. Every rule from here on has something to choose: a gap, a slope, an alarm level. Anything chosen by looking at events will score well on those events, so the events that judge the choice must be kept apart:

    • the training events, used to fit and to search;
    • the validation events, used to choose between the rules found on training;
    • the test events, used once, at the end, to report how well the chosen rule does.

    train_test_split cuts the rows at random. Explosions are only one event in ten, so a random cut can leave a part with too few; stratify= the label keeps the share of explosions the same in every part. Two cuts make the three parts: first 20 percent off for the test, then 25 percent of the rest for validation.

    The two labels, which overlapped in each magnitude alone, come apart in the two together: the explosions sit below the earthquakes. A line below Ms = mb could split them: flag an event when Ms < mb − gap. Magnitudes have one decimal, so many events would sit exactly on a gap like 1.0; gaps that end in 5 avoid that: 0.55, 0.75, 0.95, 1.15, 1.35.

    Logistic regression searches for the same kind of line, but in a different way, and it gives something the grid cannot: a probability for every event. It works out a value $z$ from the columns, as LinearRegression did, and bends $z$ into a probability with the S-curve

    $$p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \qquad z = a \times \text{mb} + b \times \text{Ms} + c$$

    where $p$ is the probability that the event is an explosion, $a$, $b$, $c$ are the three numbers fit finds, and $e \approx 2.718$. For $z = -2$, $p = 0.12$; for $z = 0$, $p = 0.5$; for $z = 2$, $p = 0.88$. The events where $z = 0$, so $p = 0.5$, lie on a straight line, the decision boundary: solved for Ms it is Ms = −(a × mb + c) / b. On one side the model says explosion, on the other earthquake.

    How fit scores a curve. Your grid scored a line by counting right and wrong. fit scores a curve by the probability it gives each event for the label it really has: $p$ for an explosion, $1 - p$ for an earthquake. Multiplied over all the events, that is the chance the curve gives to the labels coming out as they did; fit keeps the curve that makes it largest. Against the same curve moved one unit to the right:

    In [21]:
    Copied! 
    w = six_model.coef_[0][0]      # the number fit found for size
c = six_model.intercept_[0]    # and the constant
size = six_events["size"]
six_label = six_events["is_explosion"]

for name, z in [("fitted curve", w * size + c), ("curve moved right by 1", w * (size - 1) + c)]:
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))                          # the S-curve
    own = six_label * p + (1 - six_label) * (1 - p)   # p for an explosion, 1 - p for an earthquake
    chance = 1
    for q in own:
        chance = chance * q                           # multiply the six together
    print(name, ": probability of each event's own label", list(own.round(2)), " all six:", round(chance, 3))
    w = six_model.coef_[0][0] # the number fit found for size c = six_model.intercept_[0] # and the constant size = six_events["size"] six_label = six_events["is_explosion"] for name, z in [("fitted curve", w * size + c), ("curve moved right by 1", w * (size - 1) + c)]: p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)) # the S-curve own = six_label * p + (1 - six_label) * (1 - p) # p for an explosion, 1 - p for an earthquake chance = 1 for q in own: chance = chance * q # multiply the six together print(name, ": probability of each event's own label", list(own.round(2)), " all six:", round(chance, 3))

    The chance of all six falls from 0.256 to 0.152 when the curve moves: the fitted curve scores higher. (On six events this cleanly split, an ever steeper curve would score higher still; fit stops that by keeping the numbers small.) With two columns, fit does the same with $a$, $b$ and $c$.

    ✏️ Your turn 7¶

    Does fit find the grid's line, and which line does best on the validation events?

    Why: the grid searched by counting, fit by probability. If they agree, you know what fit did. The validation events, which none of the three lines saw, judge between them.

    1. model: LogisticRegression().fit(...) on the training events: mb and Ms, then the label.
    2. boundary_slope and boundary_offset: the boundary written as a line, like the grid's. a, b = model.coef_[0] and c = model.intercept_[0] are given: here a = 5.91, b = -3.31, c = -18.16. The boundary is where z = 0, so a × mb + b × Ms + c = 0. Move a × mb + c to the other side: b × Ms = −a × mb − c. Divide by b: Ms = (−a / b) × mb − c / b. So the slope is −a / b and the offset is c / b. And b is negative: a larger Ms makes an earthquake more likely. Dividing by a negative number turns > into <, so the side where z > 0, the explosions, is Ms < slope × mb − offset, the same form as the grid's line.
    3. f1_val_model: the model's F1 on the validation events, with model.predict(...). The F1s of the line by eye and the grid's line on the same events are given.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: boundary_slope, boundary_offset and f1_val_model.

    5. Where should the alarm go?¶

    predict flags an event when its probability is 0.5 or more. Nothing says 0.5 is right. A missed explosion is a secret test that got through; a false alarm accuses a state that did nothing, though an inspection team can check a flagged event by other means. The alarm level is that choice: the probability at or above which you flag an event. Lower it and you miss fewer explosions but accuse more earthquakes. It is a choice, so it is made on the validation events.

    First, the probability itself, from the three numbers fit found.

    ✏️ Your turn 8¶

    What probability does the model give each validation event?

    Why: predict_proba is the S-curve applied to z. Compute it yourself once, and check.

    2. prob_val: the S-curve of z, 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), with np.exp.
    3. The next line prints the largest difference from model.predict_proba(...)[:, 1].

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: z and prob_val.

    At 0.5 the model flags 18 of 24 validation explosions and no earthquake; at 0.3, 23 explosions for 1 false alarm, F1 0.958, the best. Below that the false alarms grow fast. 0.3 is the level.

    Each level is one trade, one point. The ROC curve draws them all at once: the share of explosions caught (up) against the share of earthquakes falsely flagged (across), one point per level. A rule that flagged events at random would catch the same share of each, on the diagonal, the coin toss; the closer the curve hugs the top left, the better the model orders the events.

    area under the curve: 0.993

    The curve climbs almost straight up: the model catches most explosions before it flags a single earthquake. The area under the curve, 0.993, is the chance that a random explosion gets a higher probability than a random earthquake: 1 for a perfect ordering, 0.5 for a coin toss. roc_auc_score computes it; the homework has you compute it yourself. The curve shows every level but chooses none: that took the validation F1.

    Every choice is now made: the line from fit, the level from validation. The test events are opened once.

    6. Does the line work somewhere new?¶

    The line was fitted on Nevada, Central Asia and Novaya Zemlya, 1970 to 1996. North Korea has tested since 2006 at a site none of those events came from. The ISC lists five of its explosions with both magnitudes: a test of the line at a place it never saw.

    The slope is the reason. North Korea's explosions are small: mb 4.8 to 5.3, but for 2017's 6.3. Their Ms sits 0.7 to 1.1 below their mb, as it does for the small explosions in the table (a median of 1.0 below). At mb 5.1 the fitted boundary flags an event only if its Ms is more than 1.5 below its mb; at mb 6.3, more than 0.57. The steep slope was learned from large explosions, and only 9 of the 117 were small. A test set drawn from the same places cannot show this; only a new place can. A better score on familiar events does not promise a better answer on new ones.

    The question, answered¶

    Mostly, with two magnitudes and an honest score. "Always earthquake" is right 0.895 of the time and finds nothing, so the scores count hits, misses and false alarms apart. A depth of 0 looks perfect only because the analyst already knew. A grid of 560 lines and logistic regression find nearly the same line through mb and Ms; the probability logistic regression adds lets the alarm be set on validation events, and on the test events, opened once, the rule catches 22 of 23 explosions with 0 false alarms. But at North Korea's small explosions the steep line misses what the plainer line catches: its slope was learned from large explosions.

    Week 9 summary¶

    The science¶

    Earthquake or nuclear explosion?
    When one label is rare, accuracy hides the misses: 'always earthquake' scores 0.895 and finds no explosion; precision, recall and F1 count the two kinds of mistake apart. Logistic regression draws a straight line through two columns and gives every event a probability; checked on events it never saw, the line through mb and Ms finds explosions that each magnitude alone misses. But its slope was learned from large explosions: at North Korea's small ones the plain line by eye does better. Where to set the alarm is a choice between missed explosions and false accusations; the ROC curve shows every choice at once, and a column that already knows the answer (a depth the analyst set to 0) is leakage, not skill.

    • Body-wave and surface-wave magnitude. Two sizes for one event: mb is read from the first, fast P wave, Ms from the slow surface waves that follow. An explosion pushes out from one small spot and makes weak surface waves for its mb; an earthquake slips along a fault and makes strong ones.
    • Baseline. Write the dumbest rule you can, first. Any model that cannot beat it is decoration.
    • Hit, miss, false alarm. A hit is an explosion you flagged, a miss an explosion you did not, a false alarm an earthquake you flagged.
    • Precision / recall. Of the ones you flagged, how many were right? Of the real ones, how many did you catch?
    • Leakage. You got 99 percent. Be suspicious. Did one of your columns already know the answer?
    • Logistic regression. The same straight line — but now it outputs a probability between 0 and 1.
    • Decision boundary. Where the model's answer flips from one label to the other — for logistic regression, always a straight line.
    • Alarm level. The probability at or above which you flag an event. Lower it and you miss fewer explosions but accuse more earthquakes.
    • ROC curve. Every alarm level at once: the share of explosions caught against the share of earthquakes falsely flagged. The closer the curve hugs the top left, the better the model.

    The code¶

    Function What it does
    Python
    list.append(x) add one item to the end of a list
    len(table) how many rows
    for x in things: do the same thing once for each item
    round(x, 1) trim a long decimal — 9.1 rather than sixteen digits
    NumPy
    mask & other_mask True only where both masks are True, the array version of and
    np.array(list) the container that does arithmetic to every number at once
    pandas
    mask.mean() the proportion of a mask that is True, in one line
    Matplotlib
    plt.plot(x, y) join points with a line — here, the coastline
    plt.scatter(x, y) a dot per pair of values
    plt.hist(x, bins=n) how one list of numbers is spread out
    plt.axvline(x) a vertical line at x, to mark a boundary on a plot
    scikit-learn
    LogisticRegression() draw the straight line that best separates two labelled groups
    accuracy_score(y, pred) the fraction it got right — useless when one label is rare
    precision_score(y, pred) of the ones it flagged, how many really were explosions
    recall_score(y, pred) of the explosions there were, how many it flagged
    f1_score(y, pred) precision and recall in one number, so two models can be compared
    train_test_split(table, test_size=0.3, random_state=n, stratify=column) cut the rows into a training part and a held-out part, keeping the share of each label
    model.fit(X, y) / model.predict(X) learn from the training rows, then predict for any rows
    confusion_matrix(y, pred) the two kinds of mistake counted apart: misses in one corner, false alarms in the other
    model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] the model's probability that each row is the True label
    roc_auc_score(y, prob) one number for the whole ROC curve: 1 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing

    Homework¶

    An agency learns from the tests it knows and must watch places it has never recorded. Here you do the whole path of class again, alone: fit on the western US (405 events, 36 explosions, almost all at the Nevada Test Site), choose the alarm level on western-US validation events, and test once on Eurasia (Central Asia and Novaya Zemlya: 713 events, 81 explosions). One step of class per Your turn: the grid, the fit and the level, the test against the baselines, and the curve of every level. Each answer cell gives the names and says what each holds; you write the code.

    The two tables come from events, which the setup cell makes: run the setup cell, then the next.

    ✏️ Your turn 12¶

    Which line does a grid find on the western training events?

    Why: the search of Your turn 6, alone, on new events.

    1. west_train, west_validation: the western-US events cut 70/30, stratified on their label, random_state=42.
    2. west_f1s: for every offset in offsets and every slope in slopes (class's grid, set again at the top of the homework), the training F1 of the line Ms < slope × mb − offset.
    3. west_best_f1, west_best_slope, west_best_offset: kept inside the loop, as in Your turn 6. The last line, given, counts how many lines share the best F1.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: west_train, west_best_slope and west_best_offset.

    west_train, west_validation = train_test_split(west_us, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=west_us["is_explosion"])
west_f1s = []
west_best_f1 = 0
for offset in offsets:

print("the western grid's line: Ms <", west_best_slope, "x mb -", west_best_offset, ", training F1", round(west_best_f1, 3))
print(west_f1s.count(west_best_f1), "lines share that F1")

    What the numbers mean. At the western level, 0.2, the model catches 77 of 81 Eurasian explosions with 12 false alarms, F1 0.906; the western grid's line scores 0.938, and the line by eye 0.859; the baselines, "always earthquake" (accuracy 0.886, nothing found) and the cut on mb (F1 0.667), are far behind. The physics travels: small surface waves for the body-wave size hold at sites the lines never saw. The level travels less well: at 0.3 Eurasia would have scored 0.944 (76 explosions, 4 false alarms). An agency would re-check the level at each new site.

    ✏️ Your turn 15¶

    How good is the western model in Eurasia at every alarm level at once?

    Why: the ROC curve of class, in the new place, and its area computed by hand: the area is the share of (explosion, earthquake) pairs that the model puts in the right order, explosion higher.

    1. eurasia_hit_shares and eurasia_false_alarm_shares: for each level in roc_levels, the share of Eurasia's explosions flagged and the share of its earthquakes flagged.
    2. auc_by_hand: over every explosion, count the earthquakes with a lower probability; add the counts; divide by (number of explosions × number of earthquakes). The next line prints roc_auc_score beside it.
    3. The figure: the curve and the diagonal.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: eurasia_hit_shares, eurasia_false_alarm_shares and auc_by_hand.

    In [42]:
    Copied! 
    roc_levels = [1.0, 0.9, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01, 0.0]     # more levels than class, for a smoother curve
eurasia_hit_shares = []
eurasia_false_alarm_shares = []
for level in roc_levels:
    flagged = prob_eurasia >= level
    eurasia_hit_shares.append((flagged & eurasia_label).sum() / eurasia_label.sum())
    eurasia_false_alarm_shares.append((flagged & (eurasia_label == False)).sum() / (eurasia_label == False).sum())

prob_explosions = prob_eurasia[eurasia_label]
prob_earthquakes = prob_eurasia[eurasia_label == False]
pairs_right = 0
for p in prob_explosions:
    pairs_right = pairs_right + (prob_earthquakes < p).sum()
auc_by_hand = pairs_right / (len(prob_explosions) * len(prob_earthquakes))
print("area under the curve: by hand", round(auc_by_hand, 3), "  roc_auc_score", round(roc_auc_score(eurasia_label, prob_eurasia), 3))

plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 5.5))
plt.plot(eurasia_false_alarm_shares, eurasia_hit_shares, marker="o", color="black", label="model fitted in the western US")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="0.6", ls="--", label="a coin toss")
plt.xlabel("share of earthquakes falsely flagged")
plt.ylabel("share of explosions caught")
plt.title("ROC curve in Eurasia")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

What changes from place to place is mostly where a fixed level falls on the curve, which is why the level of Your turn 13 had to be chosen, and then checked, place by place.
